devto.title: The Embarrassing Reason My LLM API Bill Was Double What It Should Be
devto.body:
# The Embarrassing Reason My LLM API Bill Was Double What It Should Be

I'm going to tell you something mildly humiliating.

For about six weeks, I was paying roughly double what I should have been for API calls. Not because my app grew. Not because I picked the wrong model. Because I was doing three dumb things simultaneously and they were compounding.

Here's what they were, and how I found them.

## The Investigation

I built [PromptFuel](https://promptfuel.vercel.app) partly to answer this exact question for myself. Running `promptfuel analyze` on my prompts was how I found the problem — or rather, the problems, plural.

```bash
npm install -g promptfuel
promptfuel analyze
```

## Problem 1: Paying for the Same System Prompt 800 Times a Day

My system prompt was around 800 tokens. I was constructing a fresh `messages` array on every API call without caching. So 800 tokens × every request × full price = money leaving my account at a steady and unnecessary pace.

The fix for Claude is one addition:

```python
system=[{
    "type": "text",
    "text": your_system_prompt,
    "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}
}]
```

Cache hits cost 10% of normal input price. The system prompt hadn't changed in weeks. I was paying 100% for it every time.

## Problem 2: Sending the Entire Conversation History on Every Turn

My chat interface was appending every turn to the context and sending the whole thing. By message 20, I was sending 6,000 tokens of history to process a 15-token question.

The fix:

```javascript
// Keep a rolling window of recent context
const MAX_TURNS = 8;
const messages = conversationHistory.slice(-MAX_TURNS * 2); // user + assistant pairs
```

For most conversational apps, the last 8-10 turns is enough. The model doesn't need your full transcript to answer "can you make that shorter."

## Problem 3: Redundant Instructions I'd Copy-Pasted Into Existence

I found `"respond only in valid JSON"` in my system prompt. I also found it in my user message template. And in a comment that said `// TODO: make sure JSON output is enforced`.

The model understood it the first time. I just didn't trust it.

## What the Numbers Looked Like

After fixing all three:

- Token usage down ~42%
- Response quality: unchanged
- Time spent refactoring: one afternoon

The embarrassing part isn't that I was doing these things. It's that I was doing them for six weeks before I looked.

## If You Want to Check Your Own Prompts

```bash
npm install -g promptfuel
promptfuel analyze
```

It won't roast you as hard as I just roasted myself. But it'll find the waste.

bluesky.text: my first llm app had "respond in JSON" in the system prompt, the user message, AND a comment reminding me to add it again. this is a cry for help. `promptfuel analyze` will find yours. yours is probably different but equally embarrassing.

every model leaderboard tests chatbots on SAT questions and coding puzzles. your app is not a coding puzzle. it's "why is my summary always in spanish" and "the user typed 🥴 followed by 4000 words." bench your model on that. i'll wait.

devto.title: I Tested Claude Haiku, GPT-4o Mini, and Gemini Flash on Real Tasks. Here's What Actually Happened.
devto.body:
# I Tested Claude Haiku, GPT-4o Mini, and Gemini Flash on Real Tasks. Here's What Actually Happened.

Every few weeks someone posts a new model comparison and it's always the same: benchmark scores, carefully designed test prompts, neat bar charts. Then you try the "winning" model on your actual workload and something weird happens.

I've been running all three in production for a few months. Here's what I actually found, including the parts that don't make for clean charts.

## Quick Pricing Reality Check

| Model | Input (per 1M tokens) | Context |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Haiku 4.5 | $1.00 | 200K |
| GPT-4o Mini | $0.15 | 128K |
| Gemini 1.5 Flash | $0.075 | 1M |

Gemini Flash is genuinely 13× cheaper than Haiku. That's not a rounding error. Before you immediately migrate everything: keep reading.

## What I Was Testing

Three real workloads from a side project:

1. **Document summarization** — long PDFs, messy formatting, inconsistent structure
2. **JSON extraction** — pull structured data from unstructured user input
3. **Code explanation** — explain what a function does in plain English

Not "write a poem" or "solve this logic puzzle." Real things an app might do.

## Document Summarization: Gemini Flash Wins

Flash's 1M context window is genuinely useful here, not just a spec sheet number. I was chunking documents into pieces to fit smaller context windows. With Flash I stopped doing that.

It's also significantly cheaper, which matters when you're summarizing hundreds of documents.

The catch: Flash occasionally invents a section heading that wasn't in the original. It's subtle and sounds plausible, which makes it worse. For internal tools where someone will verify the output, fine. For anything customer-facing, I'd want a review step.

## JSON Extraction: Haiku Wins, Annoyingly

I really wanted Flash to win here because of the price. It didn't.

The task: given a paragraph of user-written text, extract structured fields into a specific JSON schema. Claude Haiku followed the schema reliably. Flash followed it most of the time, but occasionally added fields that weren't in the schema, renamed fields it didn't like, or decided to nest things differently.

Each of these breaks downstream code. The debugging cost per incident outweighed the token savings.

Haiku is predictable in a way that sounds boring but is exactly what you want when you're processing thousands of records.

## Code Explanation: GPT-4o Mini Wins

This one surprised me. GPT-4o Mini is clearly well-trained on code-related tasks. Its explanations are accurate and well-structured. It also handled edge cases (unusual syntax, legacy patterns) better than the other two.

For anything code-adjacent, it's my first reach now.

## What I Actually Use

I stopped trying to find one winner and started routing:

```javascript
function pickModel(taskType, inputTokens) {
  if (taskType === 'summarize' && inputTokens > 50000) return 'gemini-1.5-flash';
  if (taskType === 'extract_json') return 'claude-haiku-4-5';
  if (taskType === 'explain_code') return 'gpt-4o-mini';
  return 'claude-haiku-4-5'; // safe default
}
```

You can check price differences before committing to a migration:

```bash
npm install -g promptfuel
promptfuel compare claude-haiku-4-5 gpt-4o-mini gemini-1.5-flash
```

## The Actual Bottom Line

- **Cheapest by far**: Gemini Flash. Use it for volume tasks where edge cases are acceptable.
- **Most format-reliable**: Claude Haiku. Use it when you need strict schema compliance.
- **Best at code**: GPT-4o Mini. Use it for anything developer-facing.

The honest answer is: don't pick one. Pick based on the task. The cost difference between routing intelligently versus defaulting to one model is real, and it compounds over time.

bluesky.text: if you're using the same claude system prompt on every request and NOT caching it, you're paying full price for text that never changes. that's like tipping your uber driver at every red light separately. `cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}`. one line. done.
bluesky.angle: prompt caching explained with a bad analogy

bluesky.text: built promptfuel because i was tired of guessing which model to use and then getting the invoice. it's free, runs in your terminal, doesn't need your api keys. no upsell. just `npm install -g promptfuel`. if you find a bug, i'm not surprised, it's a side project.

gemini flash is so cheap it feels illegal. like i keep waiting for the "just kidding" invoice. the tradeoff: it occasionally hallucinates a JSON field with quiet confidence. haiku costs more and complains less. for anything user-facing i still reach for haiku.
bluesky.angle: gemini flash price shock + real tradeoff
